source.title: A Resource Model For Neural Scaling Law
source.authors: Jinyeop Song; Zi-Ming Liu; Max Tegmark; Jeff Gore

record.file_problem: none; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper uses toy regression experiments to investigate power-law loss scaling against allocated neurons, a different setting and measure from held-out language-model loss against parameters, tokens, or compute.
record.gate_note: The paper reports toy-task loss and resource-allocation results, recorded below. Its Chinchilla comparison and LLM scaling derivation are theoretical and rely on assumptions; cited results from Hoffmann et al. are not rows.
record.test_reason: The experiments measure toy regression MSE against the number of neurons a sparsity penalty leaves active, with α (task-loss weight) as the knob. That is a related construct, not loss against parameters, tokens or compute in language models or other trained model families. The Chinchilla link (Np ∝ N³ giving ℓ ∝ Np^-1/3) is derived from three stated assumptions and compared with Hoffmann et al.'s cited exponent; no new model-size runs test it. The authors concede the agreement 'could be a pure coincidence.' The paper offers a mechanism for the scaling law rather than a test of any version, so the findings go under fits_no_version.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. In toy single, parallel and serial regression tasks the authors find loss ∝ N⁻¹ in allocated neurons and constant resource ratios across subtasks. Under three assumptions they derive ℓ ∝ Np^-1/3, matching Chinchilla's −0.34, but they note this 'could be a pure coincidence.' They frame the model as hypothesis, with extension to LLMs only hoped for.
record.recipe_differences: The paper studies sparsity-regularized toy regression networks and plots task loss against allocated neurons; it does not reproduce the language-model parameter/token/compute sweeps or held-out-loss fitting procedure of the original sources.
record.method_sensitivity: Toy-task behavior varies by target function and training phase: the serial-task curve has an initial faster-decrease phase before N⁻¹ scaling, and sin²(π(x)) is an exception to the reported asymptotic pattern. In parallel tasks, allocation and MSE ratios depend on β.

fits_no_version.finding: Single x² regression: task MSE scales roughly as N⁻¹ in allocated neurons across α∈[1,512], with 16 seeds per α.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In sparsity-regularised toy regression networks, subtask loss is roughly inversely proportional to the neurons allocated to it.

fits_no_version.finding: Across various target functions and depths 1–3, most functions show an asymptotic −1 exponent after a faster initial decrease. sin²(πx) is the exception.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The toy loss-versus-allocated-neuron exponent depends on the target function and on the regime.

fits_no_version.finding: In two parallel tasks, the allocation ratio stays at 2.35 ± 0.24 across α at β = 0.75. Allocation and MSE ratios depend on β but not on α, and composite loss scales as N⁻¹.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In toy composite tasks, subtask resource shares stay constant as total resources grow (homogeneous growth), giving N⁻¹ composite loss.

fits_no_version.finding: In the serial composite task, loss falls faster than N⁻¹ until about α = 640, then follows N⁻¹. Active neurons rise coherently across all layers.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Toy serial-task loss against allocated neurons shows two regimes rather than a single power law.

record.peer_reviewed: Published as a workshop paper at ICLR 2024
record.problems: The empirical studies use synthetic toy regression tasks, not language models or held-out pretraining loss. The connection to parameter count and the Chinchilla exponent is derived from assumptions rather than tested in new LLM runs. Many plotted relationships have no tabulated numerical fits; the text reports no control experiments.
record.rows_left_out: No empirical row is recorded for the paper's assumed derivation Np ∝ N³ and implied LLM exponent, or for its Chinchilla agreement statement: these are theoretical claims and a comparison to cited work, not a new measured language-model result.

untested.parts: No language-model (or any model-size) sweep of held-out loss against parameters, tokens or compute. Neuron count is varied via the sparsity weight α at fixed width.
No extrapolation from small fits to larger runs.
No fixed-compute parameter/token allocation. The Chinchilla exponent agreement is derived, not measured.
The critical-depth idea and width-only scaling are conjecture only. Toy depth 1–3 runs (Appendix A) are not compared at fixed parameter count.
Toy regression loss against allocated neurons is not a model-size scaling law in another modality or regime.
No fitted exponents or fitting choices are compared. Regime changes appear only in toy loss against allocated neurons.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's tranche (T2, tests) is overturned: neuron count here is set by a regularisation weight, not by model size, and no language model is trained. The width-only scaling prediction (ℓ ∝ Np^-1/2) is an untested conjecture.

versions.untested_parts: No held-out pretraining loss of language models is measured against parameter count, training tokens, or compute.
No small-run fit is tested against the loss of a substantially larger language-model run.
No fixed-compute language-model sweep over parameter and token allocations is performed.
The paper varies toy-network depth in regression experiments, but does not compare language-model architectures at fixed parameter count to test the stated claim.
No image, video, repeated-data, fine-tuning, or transfer scaling experiment is conducted.
No downstream task performance is measured.
Toy regression curves show different regimes and a task exception, but the paper does not test language-model fitted exponents, fitting choices, or compute-optimal splits.

rows.subject: fully connected network with a single hidden layer
rows.operation_detail: Varied task-loss weight α under sparsity regularization, changing the number of neurons allocated to an x² regression task; measured task MSE against allocated-neuron count.
rows.measure: Task MSE versus number of allocated neurons
rows.note: The paper describes the relationship across 16 seeds; the plotted curve does not provide a tabulated value.

rows.subject: regression networks with hidden-layer configurations [1000], [200, 200], and [150, 150, 150]
rows.operation_detail: Changed the target regression function and network depth; measured task loss against allocated-neuron count.

conditions.value: various simple regression target functions; individual function list not stated in the text

rows.value: The majority of tested functions show an asymptotic exponent of -1 after a faster-decrease phase; sin²(π(x)) is the exception.
rows.note: Reported as a summary across functions and depths; the text does not enumerate the other target functions or give per-function numerical fits.

rows.subject: single-hidden-layer network performing two parallel x² regression tasks
rows.operation_detail: Varied task intensity and relative task weights, then measured composite task loss against total allocated-neuron count.
rows.measure: Composite task loss versus total allocated neurons
rows.value: The paper reports an N⁻¹ scaling relation across the listed β values.
rows.note: No numerical fit values are stated in the text.
rows.check: The β list is inconsistent in the paper: this sentence gives 0.8, while the β sweep (R5) lists 0.85. The text also cites 'Figure 1-D' where Figure 3-D is meant. The row correctly follows the paper's 0.8, but readers should note the discrepancy.

rows.subject: single-hidden-layer network performing two parallel x² regression tasks
rows.operation_detail: Measured the ratio of neurons allocated to the two tasks while varying α.
rows.measure: Ratio of allocated neurons for the first task to the second
rows.value: 2.35 ± 0.24 across a wide range of α values
rows.note: This is a resource-allocation result in a toy task, not a parameter/token allocation result for language models.

rows.subject: single-hidden-layer network performing two parallel x² regression tasks
rows.operation_detail: Varied α and β and measured task-resource and task-loss ratios.
rows.measure: Ratio of allocated neurons and ratio of the two task MSEs
rows.value: Both ratios are reported as maintained across α and dependent on β; numerical ratios are not stated.
rows.note: The authors state that the ratios depend heavily on β but are insensitive to α.

rows.subject: four-hidden-layer network performing a serial composite regression task
rows.size_stated: Four hidden layers, each with 30 neurons
rows.operation_detail: Varied α under sparsity regularization and measured composite task loss against allocated-neuron count.

conditions.value: F(x₁, x₂, x₃, x₄) = (x₁ − x₂)² + (x₃ − x₄)²

rows.measure: Composite task loss versus allocated-neuron count
rows.value: Loss decreases faster than N⁻¹ initially, then follows N⁻¹ scaling at higher α; the text associates the transition with around α = 640.
rows.note: The authors describe two regimes: an initial phase of faster decrease and a later N⁻¹ regime.

rows.subject: four-hidden-layer network performing a serial composite regression task
rows.size_stated: Four hidden layers, each with 30 neurons
rows.operation_detail: Measured allocated/live neurons by layer as α varied.

conditions.value: varied; exact plotted values not stated

rows.measure: Number of allocated neurons in each layer
rows.note: The text states that active-neuron counts increase coherently across layers as α increases; no numerical values are given.
